definition: A manufactured fiber extruded from two polymers, or two grades of one polymer, through the same spinneret so that both run continuously along the fiber in a defined cross-sectional arrangement.
explanation: Two polymer melts are metered separately and brought together in a spin pack designed to combine them in a set geometry. In a side-by-side arrangement, the two halves shrink differently after drawing or heating, so the fiber curls into a helical crimp, loosely comparable to the bilateral cortex of crimpy wool. In a sheath-core arrangement, a low-softening sheath can bond fibers together in nonwovens while the core carries load. In islands-in-the-sea or segmented-pie designs, one component is dissolved away or the segments are split apart to produce very fine microfibers.
example: A nonwoven engineer blends sheath-core staple fibers into a batt and passes it through an oven set hot enough to soften the sheath but not the core. The sheaths fuse at fiber crossings while the cores stay solid, producing a lofty, bonded pad without any added adhesive. The example shows how two polymers in one fiber can each do a separate job.
caution: Bicomponent describes fiber construction, not a fiber blend: a blend mixes separate fibers of different types, while a bicomponent fiber combines two polymers inside each fiber. The term does not reveal which polymers are used, their proportions, or whether they can be separated for recycling. For labeling, check how the applicable fiber-naming rules treat the product rather than assuming a single generic name applies.
deeper: A review of melt-spun fibers names three main cross-sections: core-sheath, side-by-side, and multiple-core types such as segmented pie and islands-in-the-sea. The melts stay separate until the spin pack, so the filament contains unmixed components touching at an interface; the polymers need well-matched processing temperatures and viscosities and suitable adhesion. Core-sheath binder fibers pair a standard core with a low softening-point sheath that fuses in thermally bonded nonwovens. Side-by-side fibers use polymers with different shrinkage, so after heat or relaxation they curl into self-crimp. Segmented-pie fibers from poorly adhering polymers split into microfibers, and islands-in-the-sea fibers release fibrils when the sea polymer is dissolved. Functional compounds, such as conductive or antistatic additives, can be placed in one component so that the other preserves tensile strength.
origins: Bicomponent spinning grew from the aim of combining in one fiber properties that neither polymer offers alone. The review cited here dates the commercial launch of bicomponent fibers to the 1960s and notes that their range has grown considerably since. Today the main commercial roles are binder fibers for thermally bonded nonwovens, self-crimping fibers that give bulk without separate texturing, and precursors for microfibers.

definition: Able to be broken down by microorganisms into carbon dioxide, water, methane and biomass; as a marketing claim, it needs evidence tied to realistic disposal conditions.
explanation: Biodegradation is a biological process. Microbes secrete enzymes that cut polymer chains into fragments small enough to absorb and metabolize, ultimately converting the carbon to carbon dioxide with oxygen present, or to methane and carbon dioxide without it. Cellulose and protein fibers are generally susceptible because common microbial enzymes, such as cellulases and proteases, attack their bonds, while most petroleum-based synthetic fibers degrade very slowly. Rates depend on temperature, moisture, oxygen, the microbial community, fiber crystallinity, finishes and dyes. In marketing, 'biodegradable' is an environmental claim that must be substantiated for the conditions consumers would reasonably expect.
example: Two socks are advertised as 'biodegradable': one is untreated wool, the other a polyamide containing a degradation-promoting additive. A student would ask, for each, which test method was used, under what conditions and for how long, and what percentage of the material's carbon was converted. Then the key question: do those conditions resemble where used socks actually end up? The same word can rest on very different evidence.
caution: Biodegradable is not the same as compostable, which refers to a managed system with defined criteria, or bio-based, which describes where a feedstock came from. Fragmentation into smaller pieces is not biodegradation unless microbes also consume the fragments. Blends, elastane, coatings and synthetic sewing thread can stop a whole garment from biodegrading even when its main fiber would.
deeper: Laboratory evidence usually comes from respirometric tests, which measure carbon dioxide released, or oxygen consumed, by a sample held in soil, compost, sludge or seawater, and report it as a percentage of the theoretical maximum calculated from the sample's carbon content. Soil-burial tests for textiles instead track loss of tensile strength or mass, which shows deterioration but not complete mineralization. In the United States, 16 CFR 260.8 calls for competent and reliable scientific evidence that the entire item will completely break down and return to nature within a reasonably short time after customary disposal, with one year as the limit for items usually sent to landfills, incinerators or recycling facilities. In the EU, Directive (EU) 2024/825 restricts generic environmental claims from 27 September 2026.
origins: The word joins the prefix bio-, from Greek bios (life), to degradable. As the term spread through consumer marketing, regulators addressed it directly: the FTC's Green Guides, first issued in 1992, include a section on degradable claims, and the current 2012 text sets the one-year benchmark for landfill-bound items. In the EU, Directive (EU) 2024/825, adopted on 28 February 2024, amended consumer law to target unsubstantiated generic environmental claims.

definition: A wool-cleaning process that uses sulfuric acid and heat to make cellulose-based vegetable matter brittle so it can be crushed and removed from the fiber.
explanation: Scoured wool can still contain burrs, seeds and grass, and in recycled material there may be cotton or other cellulose fibers. Carbonizing exploits a chemical difference: cellulose is hydrolyzed and weakened by strong acid at elevated temperature, while wool keratin tolerates acid far better. The wool is soaked in dilute sulfuric acid, dried and baked so the vegetable matter chars and becomes friable, then passed between crushing rollers and shaken so the fragments fall out. The wool is finally rinsed and neutralized. It belongs mainly to the woollen route, whereas worsted processing relies more on carding and combing.
example: A mill receives a heavily burred lot of fine wool destined for woollen spinning. Carding alone would leave vegetable fragments in the yarn, visible later as specks in the fabric. The mill carbonizes the scoured wool first, then cards it. A student comparing samples before and after would see cleaner fiber but should also test whether strength and handle have changed.
caution: Carbonizing is not charring the wool, and it has nothing to do with making carbon fiber. It can weaken and yellow wool if acid concentration, temperature or time are excessive, and the acid must be removed carefully. In blends it destroys any cellulosic component, so it changes the fiber composition that ends up on the label.
deeper: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis cleaves the beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds of cellulose, and baking concentrates the acid as water evaporates, leaving vegetable matter brittle enough to crush. Keratin's amide backbone is far less susceptible under these conditions, and the fiber buffers acid through its amino and carboxyl groups, but protection is incomplete: carbonizing damages wool to some degree, and removing residual sulfuric acid takes large volumes of rinse water. Process control centers on acid concentration, liquor pickup, baking temperature and time. As a possible substitute, laboratory work has used fungal xylanase and cellulase to digest vegetable matter in fleece, and the authors reported removal without measurable fiber deterioration; this remains a research approach rather than standard mill practice.
origins: The name refers to the charred, carbon-like appearance of the vegetable matter after acid baking. The process belongs to the woollen side of the industry, where burrs and seeds must be removed before carding and spinning, and wool industry bodies describe it alongside scouring as part of early-stage processing. Its costs in water use and fiber damage are the main reasons researchers now test enzymatic alternatives.
